extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters, city editors, and journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what makes material 'news' for newspapers and how to structure/write stories to reach hurried, scanning readers. Covers tests of newsworthiness, local/context differences, instincts/appeal factors, avoidance of sensationalism, and practical writing constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anything
rubrics_metrics.description: "Anything." Of all publications, the newspaper alone finds use for this word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspapers can print a broad variety of material (unlike specialty magazines). This openness is a defining characteristic of the paper: it may carry travel, sports, local trivia, or world events because the paper addresses many reader interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely
rubrics_metrics.description: "Timely." The newspaper offers its readers new news, thereby differentiating itself from review, analytical, and critical publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness should be interpreted flexibly — items that become newly relevant (e.g., discovery of old events, memoir revelations) can be timely. Avoid absurd hyper-timeliness (valuing an event at 1 p.m. over noon purely for recency). Expanded foreign coverage has changed what counts as timely. Overemphasis on minute recency is a pitfall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interests
rubrics_metrics.description: "Interests." A piece of news need not instruct, amuse, inform, or exhort; it is good if it be interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News judged by interest can include trivial or inconsequential items because newspapers aim to mirror life. Specialized papers may emphasize 'constructive' or 'permanent' news for a limited clientele, but general papers must often include items whose chief merit is interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number (aim at many readers)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Number." Newspapers, unless they limit themselves, attempt to find readers from all groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate news in terms of community-wide appeal rather than narrow specialist interest. General papers must consider bishops and butlers, professors and plumbers; what matters is whether the item will attract readers across many segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readers' identification (universal test of news worth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter has one reasonably definite and universal test for news worth — the extent to which readers will identify themselves with the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'common-denominator' test—how many and how vigorously readers see the story as related to their interests—is the natural system for assessing relative news value instead of artificial category scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared participation
rubrics_metrics.description: A happening in which the reader shared or participated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events readers directly experienced (e.g., a local storm) are strong news because readers want to relive, get a fuller picture, or compare the reporter's account with their own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watched events
rubrics_metrics.description: An event which readers watched, though they did not take part in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large public spectacles (parades, local ceremonies) attract readers who watched and want to see whether the reporter noticed certain details; high spectator counts increase news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-known person or place
rubrics_metrics.description: News concerning a well-known person or place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories about familiar local characters or landmarks draw attention because readers recognize names or places; even small incidents become news when they involve recognized figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel-field interest
rubrics_metrics.description: News of a field parallel to one in which readers themselves are interested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groups identify with achievements in related communities (e.g., one denomination reading about another's mortgage burning-off). Parallel-field stories extend interest beyond direct participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fascinating or evocative names
rubrics_metrics.description: A name gleaming with mystery, romance, intrigue, or other fascination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A striking or glamorous name (or connection to celebrity/romance) can make an otherwise small item compelling to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation or clarification
rubrics_metrics.description: The news that interprets or clarifies a little understood action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytic 'second-day' stories that explain implications (who pays tariff changes, what a policy means) are valuable even if the facts were reported earlier; these pieces often suffer undervaluation, yet they deepen readers' understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic/universal interest (instincts)
rubrics_metrics.description: News of 'automatic' interest because it stirs or appeals to some trait or concern found in many readers as to be 'general' or 'universal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional 'instincts' include conflict/competition, sympathy, children, animals, romance, mystery, sex, adventure, heroism, etc. These instincts vary regionally and by publication; lists of instincts help but overlapping instincts and varying rankings make strict scoring artificial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict/competition as high-interest element
rubrics_metrics.description: Among 'automatically interesting' subjects is 'conflict,' or 'struggle,' or 'competition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories emphasizing struggle (sports, legal fights) attract readers, but reporters must avoid overplaying minor confrontations by forcing the 'fight' into the lead when it's not central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy and human-interest triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Sympathy' is another instinct. An emotionally moving incident, well described, always is worth space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human-interest items (rescues, tragedies, personal appeals) have lasting appeal; examples include widely distributed short animal-rescue stories. Use sympathy carefully without sensationalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names make news (tradition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the traditions that deserve longevity is the one that 'names make news.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more names appearing in a story, the better — readers look for their own names or acquaintances; lists of attendees or local names increase immediate reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: News without events (trends, conditions, interpretations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trends, conditions, situations, and interpretations are news even when 'nothing happened.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forecasts, business outlooks, cultural trends, and topics people will talk about tomorrow are newsworthy. A reporter's ability to spot or predict such topics in advance marks a strong journalist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing/quality of reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: An event itself is news, but many a trifling event has become powerful news because of the way it was written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good reporting and intelligent processing (finding parallels, adding context or human detail) can elevate routine items into compelling copy; 'processing' is a major sales appeal of a newspaper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local context: metropolis vs small city and group interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual city and surroundings exercise a powerful influence upon news values: in the 'big town' the unusual is news; in the 'village' the familiar or routine is news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust news judgment to community size and composition: metropolitan readers require more novelty or big names, while small communities value routine and familiar figures. Also consider ideological/group interests that shape what a paper emphasizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reexamine worn-out traditions/fetishes
rubrics_metrics.description: Within every office there are certain fetishes, certain beliefs as to news values, that have been handed down from the past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditions (e.g., 'first person hit by a trolley is front-page news') may be outdated; editors/reporters should reassess inherited rules and discard those no longer valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume 'heavy stuff' is weak news
rubrics_metrics.description: Most dangerous of the fetishes is the one that 'heavy stuff' is weak news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serious, complex subjects (economics, history, finance, foreign affairs) can attract and satisfy readers if well written; tabloid assumptions about readers' limited comprehension are misleading. Quality journalism that explains 'heavy' topics can strengthen circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensationalism / 'waves of yellow' journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: News sometimes runs in waves or cycles of sensational or 'yellow' journalism; these are usually artificial and temporary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While yellow cycles can bring short-term circulation gains, the public eventually tires and returns to regular journalism. Excessive sensationalism may alienate mainstream, profitable readers and harm long-term prestige and profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard story structure (write for the worst/bad readers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspaper writing has a 'standard form' or 'standard structure' that accounts for the way a newspaper is read and written; it enables hurried, scanning readers to grasp a story in a few glances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the standard structure especially for straight news: craft a strong lead, organize key facts up front, and write so that readers can obtain the main points in 5–6 eye movements. Even stylish reporters use the standard form when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability constraints (short paragraphs, narrow columns, small type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspaper columns are narrow and type small; paragraphs must be short, else they become illegible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write concise paragraphs, favor short sentences and active constructions, and structure copy for narrow column widths and small type. These physical constraints demand superlative clarity of writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline importance
rubrics_metrics.description: The headline can convey the story; if it is well written, many readers will obtain all they wish to know from it and will read little of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft headlines that capture the essential news and entice further reading; recognize that a strong headline can serve many scanning readers who won't read beyond the lead paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production realities: speed and first-draft correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter must write rapidly and 'write correctly the first time' even though occasional quick races with the clock occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to produce accurate copy quickly; while not every story is written in panic conditions, reporters should avoid habitual slow performance and strive for accuracy with minimal rewrites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spotting/timing stories (anticipation of topics people will discuss)
rubrics_metrics.description: What people are talking about or will talk about tomorrow is news; ability to spot such topics, especially in advance, is the mark of a good reporter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop contacts and judgment to predict which occurrences or trends will become topics of widespread conversation; early identification and context-building yield strong stories.
